summary: Extends IKEv2 so that more than one key exchange can contribute to the shared secret during security association setup, using the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange and a new IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchange for rekeying. It is aimed at hybrid and post-quantum key exchange.

plainLanguage.summary: To make a secret lock safer, two people mix several secret recipes together, so it stays safe even if one recipe gets cracked later.

questions: how to do post-quantum key exchange in ikev2
what is ikev2 multiple key exchange
how does ikev2 support post-quantum key exchange
subtitle: How IKEv2 can run several key exchanges in a row so the session key survives a quantum computer.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 relies on (EC)DH, which is believed to be breakable by quantum computers, and post-quantum key exchanges are too new to trust alone and often too large for IKE_SA_INIT messages.
tldr.mechanism: Seven new transform types negotiate extra key exchanges, which run in IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges at SA setup and in the new IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchange for CREATE_CHILD_SA, with keys updated after each one.
tldr.outcome: The final keys depend on every exchange, so they stay secure if any one of them is secure. RFC 9370 updates RFC 7296.

facts.label: Payload size limit
facts.value: KE payloads over 64 KB not addressed

today: RFC 9370 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2023. It updates RFC 7296 by renaming Transform Type 4 and the Key Exchange payload field, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Quantum Problem
sections.content:
IKEv2 (RFC 7296) uses Diffie-Hellman or Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman, written (EC)DH, to establish a shared secret. It is believed that general-purpose quantum computers will be able to solve the underlying problem, which would compromise IKEv2. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) covers algorithms conjectured to resist such attacks.

No post-quantum key exchange is yet as well studied as (EC)DH. So the RFC lets peers combine several key exchanges, for example classical plus post-quantum, so that the overall security is at least as strong as each individual primitive. The same approach also works when all exchanges are classical, for instance for policy reasons.

The RFC calls itself a long-term solution. A short-term option is post-quantum pre-shared keys, as in RFC 8784. It does not address key exchange payloads longer than 64 KB, because the IKE payload format does not allow them.
sections.plainLanguage: A lock that is safe today might be pickable by a future machine. So you put several different locks on the door, and a thief has to pick all of them.

sections.title: Negotiating Extra Key Exchanges
sections.content:
The normal key exchange is still negotiated with Transform Type 4 (renamed from "Diffie-Hellman Group" to "Key Exchange Method") and still happens in IKE_SA_INIT. Extra ones use seven new transform types, ADDKE1 to ADDKE7, with IANA values 6 to 12. They share the Transform ID registry of Transform Type 4, so any method, classical or post-quantum, can be used in any slot.

The initiator may include any of the ADDKE types. If it includes none, the proposal means standard IKEv2. If it includes one, the responder MUST select one of the algorithms proposed for it. The Transform ID NONE can be added to mark an exchange as optional, and omitted ADDKE types are treated as NONE. The responder's choice MUST NOT contain duplicate algorithms, except NONE. If it cannot choose without duplicates, it MUST reject with NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN.

An initiator that includes ADDKE types MUST also send the INTERMEDIATE_EXCHANGE_SUPPORTED notification from RFC 9242, and the responder MUST return it if it agrees. Without that, peers treat ADDKE types as unknown and skip the proposals that contain them.
sections.plainLanguage: When two people agree how to lock a door, one can say which extra locks to add and in what order. Each side picks from the list, and they may not pick the same lock twice.

sections.title: Additional Exchanges During SA Setup
sections.content:
Large post-quantum keys may not fit in IKE_SA_INIT, which has no fragmentation support. So the extra exchanges run as IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges after IKE_SA_INIT and before IKE_AUTH. These are encrypted, so IKE fragmentation (RFC 7383) can be used. Extra exchanges run in order of their transform type values, and each MUST be fully completed before the next starts. Each exchange carries KEi(n) and KEr(n) payloads whose Key Exchange Method field MUST match the n-th negotiated method.

After each exchange both sides recompute keys: SKEYSEED(n) = prf(SK_d(n-1), SK(n) | Ni | Nr), then derive SK_d, SK_ai, SK_ar, SK_ei, SK_er, SK_pi and SK_pr from it. The next exchange uses the updated keys. Because the chain feeds forward, the final IKE SA keys depend on all exchanges. IKE_AUTH then proceeds as usual, with the AUTH payload calculation from RFC 9242.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new secret is stirred into the pot, and the next step uses the freshly stirred pot. By the end, the final secret depends on every ingredient.

sections.title: Rekeying with IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE
sections.content:
CREATE_CHILD_SA creates or rekeys Child SAs and rekeys the IKE SA. For these, additional key exchanges run as a series of new IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchanges (Exchange Type 44) after the CREATE_CHILD_SA. Since several exchanges can be in flight on an established IKE SA, a new status notification, ADDITIONAL_KEY_EXCHANGE (type 16441), links them. The responder fills it with an opaque blob and the initiator MUST echo it back intact in the next request.

If the initiator disappears, the responder MUST delete the state after a reasonable time; the RFC says 5 to 20 seconds is generally appropriate. If an IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE arrives for which no state exists, the responder MUST answer with the error STATE_NOT_FOUND (type 47), which is not fatal to the IKE SA. The initiator then treats the whole series as failed, and may retry with a new CREATE_CHILD_SA. If it keeps getting STATE_NOT_FOUND after several retries, it MUST treat that as fatal and delete the IKE SA.

Keys combine all the secrets. For an IKE SA rekey: SKEYSEED = prf(SK_d, SK(0) | Ni | Nr | SK(1) | ... SK(n)). For Child SAs: KEYMAT = prf+ (SK_d, SK(0) | Ni | Nr | SK(1) | ... SK(n)).

Simultaneous rekeying changes slightly: no SA exists yet when CREATE_CHILD_SA completes, so the initiator of the exchange with the smallest nonce just stops, and MUST NOT start IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE. A request to rekey an SA already being rekeyed gets a TEMPORARY_FAILURE notification.
sections.plainLanguage: When the locks are changed on a door already in use, the extra locks are added in small follow-up visits. A ticket number ties the visits together, and if the visitor takes too long the first person forgets about the job.

sections.title: Childless IKE SAs and Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC believes no other IKEv2 extension needs changing; IKE SA resumption (RFC 5723) can resume SAs made this way.

One interaction needs care. The first Child SA created in IKE_AUTH is protected only by the initial exchange, so with a classical IKE_SA_INIT method it offers no resistance against quantum attack. To avoid this, peers can use childless IKE SA (RFC 6023): the initiator offers proposals with and without ADDKE types, the responder picks the one without and signals CHILDLESS_IKEV2_SUPPORTED, no Child SA is made in IKE_AUTH, and the peers immediately rekey the IKE SA and create Child SAs with additional key exchanges. Support for this mode is not negotiated, so the responder cannot force it.

Sensitive data sent over the initial IKE SA is not protected by the additional exchanges, so in that case a post-quantum algorithm should be used in Transform Type 4.
sections.plainLanguage: The very first door installed before the extra locks arrive stays weak. So it is better to install the door and then upgrade the locks before using it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension targets two threats: the break of (EC)DH by Shor's algorithm, and the possible break of a new PQC algorithm. The main goal is to stop "harvest-and-decrypt" attacks, where an attacker records traffic now and decrypts it later with a quantum computer. The hybrid design prevents this as long as the PRF is quantum resistant.

Active quantum attackers are not completely addressed, because authentication remains classical. A long pre-shared key is post-quantum secure, but signature algorithms in common use are not. Post-quantum authenticity would need a post-quantum signature.

The encryption, PRF and integrity transforms are not susceptible to Shor's algorithm, but are to Grover's attack. According to NIST, AES with a minimum key length of 128 bits can continue to be used, though longer keys may be wise for data that must stay secret for many years. Ordering of the extra exchanges should not matter in general, though an implementer may prefer to run the most secure method first.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra locks stop someone who copies your sealed messages today and opens them in the future. They do not yet prove who you are, because that part still uses the old method.
